Essentials 2.0 · Flow inspiration · 03-scenario-manager

Scenario manager: ideas from other products

This page shows examples from other products for the Scenario manager in Essentials 2.0, grouped by product. They cover creating, editing and retiring reusable scenarios, equipment lists with setup notes, and who can access each scenario. They also cover simple checklists and who fills them in, and feedback checklists opened by QR code on a phone without logging in. Other topics are scripts for the simulator and the standardized patient (SP), orientation and pre-briefing material, and what should happen automatically for each scenario. Adding scenarios to a course is in courses/05-scenarios, roles and sharing are in the user-management research, and equipment stock is in 05-inventory. Sources: the design reference libraries Mobbin and Refero, researched on 30 September 2026.

What we have today. Today's Essentials editor for a Simulated Clinical Experience (SCE) is a form with tabs: Details, Objectives, Patient, Briefing, and Equipment & Supplies with setup notes for the tech. It exports to PDF or to a Maestro file. Its builder for simulator stages is a subset of Laerdal Maestro, and its checklist editor is a cut-down version of the Enterprise Case Manager. Scheduling templates can send prep emails automatically, and start recording and announcements for each phase. Customers still write scenarios in Word or on paper, and closing a checklist window loses its data. The plan is a deliberately basic scenario manager, linked to inventory, with integration with SimCreate instead of a new Maestro. It adds simpler sharing and a new interactive maker for orientation and pre-briefing. Learners or faculty open checklists from a QR code on the room TV, optionally without logging in.

How to read this page

Each section below is one product. Each strip of screenshots is one flow: a real sequence of screens, in the order a user sees them. Click a screenshot to enlarge it. "Worth borrowing" lists ideas we could use, and "Avoid" lists what we should not copy. Use the task filters to see only one task, and click ☆ on a flow to add it to your own shortlist.

13 products · 21 flows · 131 screens · 8 tasks

What the best products have in common

  1. Access is chosen when the template is saved, in plain words ClickUp puts a 'Share with' choice ('All members' / 'Only me' / 'Select people' / 'Admins only') inside the 'Save as Template' pop-up, with public sharing off by default. Heidi uses three cards and spells out that team members can use a template but not edit it. Pitch asks Publish or Keep draft before a template reaches workspace members. For Essentials this suggests a small visibility setting on the scenario itself (private, my team can use, editors) instead of a separate permissions screen. Heidi's moderated public Community is not needed.See: ClickUp: Saving as a template · Heidi: Updating a template visibility · Pitch: Create branded template
  2. Draft is a visible status; publishing is a deliberate step Pitch shows a 'You are editing a template' banner the whole time, plus Draft labels. Tally keeps Draft, Preview and Publish in the header. Resend adds 'Publish New Version' with a check for warnings, and a revert that stays in Draft. Scenarios used by running courses need the same separation: faculty can edit freely while the published version keeps running. None of the flows shows what happens to existing copies or courses when a new version is published.See: Pitch: Create branded template · Tally: Creating a form · Resend: Creating a template · Resend: Restoring a version
  3. Create from something that already exists Heidi duplicates from the menu on a library row without opening the editor, names the copy '(Copy)' and confirms with a short pop-up message. Pitch and Tally let you choose 'start from scratch' or 'use a template' on the blank page. ClickUp's 'Save as Template' turns a working document into a reusable one and offers 'update existing' or 'save as new'. This answers the problem that customers write scenarios in Word: start from a colleague's scenario, not an empty form with tabs.See: Heidi: Duplicating a template · Pitch: Create branded template · Tally: Creating a form · ClickUp: Saving as a template
  4. Rules attach to the template type and say where they are active Cal.com's workflow asks 'Which event type will this apply to?', offers 'Apply to all, including future event types' and lists 'Active on N event types'. ClickUp writes the When/Then rule back as a sentence and has an on/off switch for each rule. It also warns straight away when an action will be skipped because someone lacks access. For Essentials that means a short When/Do list on the scenario, with presets and an 'active on' count: auto-record at phase start, a prep email X days before, an announcement. It does not need a general automation product.See: Cal.com: Creating a workflow · ClickUp: Creating an automation
  5. Equipment: pick from a catalog, allow free text, keep notes beside the list Shopify offers 'Search', 'Browse' and 'Add custom item' in one row, shows availability per variant in the picker and keeps a Notes box next to the items. Instacart shows popular items before you type, lets you pick several then tap Done, and has a 'Buy it again' tab to reuse earlier lists. Linking the list to Inventory items while still allowing a custom line covers centers whose inventory is incomplete. The setup notes for the tech belong next to the list, not in another tab.See: Shopify: Create and save draft order · Instacart: Creating a list
  6. Scripts sit beside what they cue, labelled by role Pitch attaches notes to one slide in a side panel and shows a dot when notes exist. Google AI Studio labels each line with a colour-coded speaker, renames a role once for all lines and keeps general style instructions apart from the lines. In Arcade, the text on each clickable spot drives the narration and can jump to another step. Together they point to a basic script per phase and per role (SP, operator) with simple 'go to' branching, without a Maestro-style stage editor.See: Pitch: Adding a speaker note · Google AI Studio: Adding dialogue · Arcade: Generating a voiceover (hotspot)
  7. Orientation is a set of blocks, with editing, preview and completion in one place Arcade starts with a choice of source (record, upload, or turn a video into a demo). It then keeps Edit, Preview and Insights together on one project, down to drop-off for each step. Teachable adds blocks from a panel that groups content blocks and a quiz, and its lesson list shows whether a lesson is empty. For the pre-briefing maker, this means an ordered set of blocks with a preview for learners. Blocks could be the existing video, text, a click-through of the room or simulator, and a short knowledge check. Completion data per step could show faculty who has done the pre-brief.See: Arcade: Creating an interactive demo · Teachable: Adding a text and image block · Teachable: Adding a quiz
  8. Checklists: required items and who fills them are captured; shared item banks are not Tally marks required items with asterisks and adds When/Then logic under a field. ClickUp gives each checklist item an assignee and a 'Use Template' action, and Teachable marks correct answers per question. The products differ on reuse: ClickUp reuses whole checklists, Teachable adds questions one at a time, and none shows an item bank shared across templates. For the person filling it in, Tally's form needs no account and ends on a plain thank-you page. Typeform makes a downloadable QR code in the same Share area as the link.See: Tally: Creating a form · ClickUp: Creating checklists · Teachable: Adding a quiz · Typeform: Share

Questions we still need to answer

  • Gap: no flow here shows the whole room-TV loop, from a QR code on a shared screen to a phone form with no login and a confirmation. Typeform shows only the author side (link and downloadable QR code). Tally shows only a no-account form with a thank-you page, on desktop. Luma is the reverse case: the host scans the guest. A targeted search for this gap found only in-app surveys that require login. How a no-login answer is tied to the right session and learner is still an Essentials design decision. Options are a code in the web address, a name field, or a room or session token.
  • Checklist editor: its own module, or part of the scenario? ClickUp keeps checklists on the item and reuses them with 'Use Template', Teachable builds a quiz inside a lesson, and Tally builds standalone forms. No product here shows one item bank reused across many templates. The evidence leans toward a checklist library that scenarios point to, so one fix updates every scenario. Who owns that library is a product decision.
  • Versions and running courses: Pitch, Tally and Resend make draft versus published explicit, and Resend restores old versions without deleting the current one. None shows what happens to courses, copies or scheduled sessions that already use a template when a new version is published. The courses/05-scenarios report raised the same open question: pin a version, make a copy, or keep a live link.
  • Automation scope: Cal.com and ClickUp only automate emails, assignees and fields. Nothing here sets physical room actions per template, such as auto-record, room announcements or learner tagging, and today these live on scheduling templates. Decide whether they move to the scenario, stay on the schedule, or come from scenario defaults that the schedule can override.
  • Equipment and Inventory: Shopify's picker shows availability per variant, which is tempting, but stock and check-out belong to 05-inventory. Decide whether the scenario list shows availability for the scheduled date, or only the item, its quantity and the tech's setup notes, with printing and prep sheets left to Inventory.

ClickUp

Same task, different field3 flows

ClickUp is the only product that covers four of these tasks. It has 'Save as Template' with 'Share with' choices in the same pop-up window, and checklists with an assignee per item and 'Use Template'. Its When/Then automations come with a plain-language summary and an 'Active' switch.

WebMobbin10 steps

Saving as a template

From an open Doc, the user opens Templates, chooses 'Save as Template', fills in the details, saves, and sees a success message with a link to Template Center.

Add, edit and delete scenariosGive access to specific scenarios

Worth borrowing

  • The save pop-up has 'Share with' choices: 'All members', 'Only me', 'Select people', 'Admins only', and 'Everyone (incl. guests)', with public sharing off by default.
  • The footer offers 'Update an existing Template' or 'Save as new' in the same pop-up.
  • 'Save Template' stays disabled until the template is named, and the empty field gets a red border.
  • The success message names the template and links 'Open in Template Center'.

Avoid

  • A public sharing switch that creates an outside link is too open for clinical scenarios, which are the center's own work.

What it means for Essentials Scenario manager: add 'save as template' with access set per template (private, chosen people, or the whole organization). That is simpler than today's unclear SCE permissions.

WebMobbin5 steps

Creating checklists

On a task detail, the user creates a checklist, adds items with per-item assignees, sees progress 0/N and a 'Use Template' option, alongside assigned comments and attachments.

Add simple checklists to scenarios

Worth borrowing

  • Each checklist row has its own assignee, so tasks can be split between roles such as the sim tech and faculty.
  • The section header shows progress ('Checklists 0/N') and a filter for the items assigned to you ('N for me').
  • 'Use Template' sits beside 'Add checklist', so a set of items can be reused on other tasks.
  • '+ New checklist item' adds a row without leaving the task.

Avoid

  • There is no scoring, no required flag and no rubric weighting, which is too thin for learner evaluation checklists.

What it means for Essentials Scenario manager: extend the cut-down Case Manager checklist with assignees and reusable templates. Essentials evaluations would still need scoring and a set time for filling them in, and this does not cover QR without login.

WebMobbin10 steps

Creating an automation

From a space Overview, the user opens Automations, builds a When/Then rule, creates it, and manages it with an on/off switch.

Choose what happens automatically for each scenario

Worth borrowing

  • The When/Then blocks are summed up in one plain sentence under the work area.
  • A warning appears right away when an action will be skipped because the assignee lacks access.
  • The assignee picker includes roles that fill themselves in, such as 'Task creator', 'Triggered by' and 'Watchers'.
  • After a rule is created, the Manage tab shows how many rules are active or inactive, with an on/off switch for each.

Avoid

  • Full libraries of integrations and rule catalogs across many categories are heavier than the few defaults a scenario needs (auto-record, prep email, announcements).

What it means for Essentials Scenario manager: turn today's auto-record, email and announcement settings on scheduling templates into a clear When/Then panel of defaults per scenario. Keep the presets few; this is not a general automation product.

Heidi

Close match2 flows

Heidi's clinical note templates offer three access options: 'Team can use but not edit', 'Community' and 'Only me'. A one-click 'Duplicate' in the library list adds '(Copy)' to the name. It is the clearest model for simpler sharing per scenario.

WebMobbin4 steps

Updating a template visibility

From the library row menu, the user opens 'Edit visibility', picks Team, Community or Only me, saves, and sees 'Community In review' plus a success message.

Give access to specific scenarios

Worth borrowing

  • Three cards set access: Team (can use, not edit), Community, and Only me.
  • The Team option says plainly that team members can use the template but not edit it.
  • Choosing Community shows an 'In review' label on the list after saving, because the community is moderated.
  • A 'Highlight your contribution' switch decides whether your name is shown publicly.

Avoid

  • Publishing to a public community of all product users is wrong for Essentials, which needs sharing by organization and role, not a global template marketplace.

What it means for Essentials Scenario manager: the best nearby model for simpler sharing per scenario (private, team can use only, or a moderated organization library) instead of today's unclear SCE access.

Cal.com

Same task, different field1 flow

In Cal.com you build a workflow once and attach it to selected event types. It offers 'Apply to all, including future event types' and shows where it is 'Active on N event types'. That is exactly a rule set on the template and applied to every run.

WebMobbin12 steps

Creating a workflow

From empty Workflows, the user builds a 'Pre-call Disclaimer' workflow, attaches it to event types, adds emails, and saves it.

Choose what happens automatically for each scenario

Worth borrowing

  • A multiple-choice list asks 'Which event type will this apply to?', next to 'Apply to all, including future event types' (screens 3-7).
  • The rule reads top to bottom: when it runs (before the start, plus an offset), then 'Do this' action cards (screens 3-8).
  • Placeholders such as {EVENT_NAME} and {ATTENDEE} fill in the email subject and text (screens 8, 10).
  • The list card shows what triggers the workflow and says 'Active on N event type' (screen 12).

Avoid

  • Across 12 screens it only offers reminders by email or text message, with none of the auto-record or announcement actions Essentials needs per phase.

What it means for Essentials Scenario manager: the best match for automation per scenario. A reusable When/Do rule set is attached to chosen event types, like SCE templates, and covers today's prep-email and auto-record defaults.

Shopify

Same task, different field1 flow

Shopify's draft orders let you add items with 'Search', 'Browse' or 'Add custom item' from one row. The picker shows availability and quantities per variant, and a Notes box sits beside the list. It is the best model for an equipment list linked to inventory that still allows free text.

WebRefero8 steps

Create and save draft order

From empty Orders, the admin creates an order, picks product variants, sets quantities and customer on a draft, saves as draft #D1, and sees it Open on the Drafts list.

Add an equipment list to a scenarioAdd, edit and delete scenarios

Worth borrowing

  • The Products area has 'Search', 'Browse' and 'Add custom item' in one row, so catalog items and free text sit together.
  • The product picker shows how many of each variant are available, keeps 'Add' disabled until something is chosen, and counts selections out of 500.
  • An unsaved draft offers 'Discard' or 'Save'; once saved, 'Duplicate' and 'Share' sit at the top of the draft.
  • A Notes box sits to the right of the items, so setup notes stay next to the equipment list.

Avoid

  • Payment, invoice and 'Mark as paid' controls belong to selling and clash with a sim equipment list.

What it means for Essentials Scenario manager: the best model to replace the free-text Equipment & Supplies field with items linked to inventory, quantities and notes. Check-out stays in Inventory, and the draft stage extends SCE editing.

Outside idea2 flows

Arcade makes interactive walkthroughs, which fits orientation. You choose how to start (record, upload, or turn a video into a demo), then work in Edit, Preview and Insights tabs that show drop-off for each step. WebMobbin8 steps

Creating an interactive demo

From the library, the user picks how to create a demo, fills in a step, sets preview options, then reviews engagement and where viewers drop off at each step.

Add orientation material

Worth borrowing

  • The start screen groups the recording options ('Chrome Extension', 'Desktop App') under a Popular label, next to uploading or turning a video into a demo (screen 2).
  • An empty step offers two sets of sources: add from your computer, the library or another demo, or capture with the extension, desktop app or Figma (screen 3).
  • Edit, Preview and Insights tabs keep editing, the learner's view and completion data in one project (screens 4-8).
  • A chart shows how many viewers carry on or drop off at each step ('From Step N: conversion / drop-off %') (screen 8).

Avoid

  • Sample data and an Upgrade banner at the end of editing are a warning: completion data for the pre-brief should not sit behind a paywall (screens 6-8).

What it means for Essentials Scenario manager: grow today's Briefing tab video into the planned interactive orientation and pre-brief maker, with an outline and clickable spots. The preview switches map to what learners see before a session. Do not copy Arcade's sales-demo insights and buttons wholesale.

Generating a voiceover (hotspot)

On a demo step, the user edits the text of a clickable callout, generates a voiceover from that text, then reviews the voiceover timeline with 'Edit voiceover'.

Add orientation materialAdd scripts (simulator, SP)

Worth borrowing

  • The written callout text is the only source for 'Generate voiceover', so one script drives both the caption and the audio (screen 1).

Create branded template

From an empty Templates library, the user names a new template, sets colors and fonts, edits it, and chooses to publish or keep as draft.

Add, edit and delete scenarios

Worth borrowing

  • Before any templates exist, the screen explains why they help and offers 'Create' twice, at the top and in the middle (screen 1).
  • The new-template pop-up asks for a name first, then offers 'Build branded' or 'Customize from gallery' (screens 2-3).
  • Previews of each slide type (chart, sample, text) update live while you set brand colours and upload a font (screens 4-7).
  • A 'You are editing a template' banner stays visible, 'Publish this template?' offers Keep draft or Publish, and library cards then show a Draft label (screens 8-10).

Avoid

  • A full presentation style builder (fonts, chart styles, slide layouts) is too much for the deliberately basic SCE editor, which should not become a Maestro-style tool.

What it means for Essentials Scenario manager: a strong pattern for scenarios in an organization library: start blank or from the gallery, keep drafts apart from published versions, and share on publish. It extends today's SCE editor without turning it into a slide product.

Close match2 flows

Tally is a form builder that works like a document, with Draft, Preview and Publish, asterisks for required items, and When/Then logic under a field. Its feedback form needs no account and ends on a plain thank-you page, which is the respondent side a QR checklist needs.

Creating a form

From an empty forms page, the author creates a form in a builder that works like a document. They add fields (text, required marks, logic, a grid, a rating) and keep it in Draft, ready to publish.

Add simple checklists to scenarios

Worth borrowing

WebMobbin4 steps

Adding dialogue

In a multi-speaker playground, the user writes a dialogue with general style instructions, alternating lines for Speaker 1 and Speaker 2, and a name and voice for each speaker.

Add scripts (simulator, SP)

Worth borrowing

  • General style instructions stay separate from each speaker's lines.
  • Each line has a colour-coded speaker label, and '+ Add dialog' adds the next line.
  • A settings panel on the right renames a role once and picks its voice, and every line updates.
  • A plain-text view next to the script builder can serve as a printable cue card.

Avoid

  • The text-to-speech voice settings and the Run button that generates audio are not needed, because Essentials needs cue cards for people (SP, operator), not synthetic speech.

What it means for Essentials Scenario manager: a deliberately basic script builder per role for SP and sim-operator lines, in line with the plan not to build a Maestro editor or a stage machine.

Instacart

Same task, different field1 flow

Instacart builds a named list with a description from catalog search. It shows popular items before you type and lets you pick several, then tap Done. A 'Buy it again' tab helps reuse, and the list header has lock and share options.

WebMobbin10 steps

Creating a list

From an empty Lists page, the user names a list with a description, picks items from the catalog, and saves the list.

Add an equipment list to a scenarioGive access to specific scenarios

Worth borrowing

  • The empty Lists page has 'Create' in two places (the header and a link on the page), so it is never hidden.
  • The add-items pop-up has 'Current list' and 'Buy it again' tabs, and an empty 'Buy it again' tab offers to browse categories.
  • Search shows popular items with pictures before you type, and you tick several before tapping Done.
  • The list header has lock and share options, and the description under the title works like setup notes.

Avoid

  • Having to choose a cover photo before adding items is an extra step a tech's prep list does not need.

What it means for Essentials Scenario manager: move today's free-text Equipment & Supplies toward picking from a catalog into a named list with notes. Stock and check-out stay in Inventory, as planned.

Luma

Same task, different field1 flow

Luma is the example of what not to do for the QR task, because the host's phone scans the guest's ticket QR code. That is the reverse of a learner's phone reading a QR code on the room TV. Its confirm-then-message steps do suit check-in by staff.

iOSMobbin3 stepsExample of what not to do

Checking in a guest (scan QR code)

An event host opens the check-in scanner, points the camera at a guest's QR code, confirms the guest's details, and checks them in.

Feedback checklist by QR code, without login

Worth borrowing

  • Clear wording ('Point the camera at a ticket QR code') tells the host exactly what to scan (screens 1, 3).
  • A panel shows the guest's name, email and status before 'Check In' is tapped (screen 2).
  • A short 'Guest checked in' message appears while the scanner stays open, which keeps a queue moving (screen 3).
  • A switch between List and Scan, plus search, gives a way out when scanning fails (screens 1, 3).

Avoid

  • Using a host who scans guest tickets as the model for room-TV feedback gets it backwards, because the wrong person holds the code.

What it means for Essentials Scenario manager: the opposite of the Essentials QR checklist, where a learner's phone reads a QR code on the TV without login. It is only loosely relevant to staff checking attendance at the door.
